Justice Scalia’s Decker separation-of-powers critique of Auer was 
previously articulated by Professor John Manning in Corvstitutional Structure 
and Judicial Deference to Agency Interpretation of Agency Rules, 96 COLUM. L. 
Re v . 612 (1996). Two years before Kisor, Professors Cass Sunstein and Adrian 
Vermeule responded to the critique, claiming that agencies did not unlawfully 
enhance their power when they interpreted their own rules. See The 
Unbearable Rightness of Auer, 84 U. CHI. L. Re v . 297 (2017). In Kisor, Justice 
Kagan relied on this article in rejecting the challenge to Auer deference.
4. 
Express Regulatory Delegations. Recall that in Loper Bright, the 
Court acknowledged that some statutes may “‘expressly delegate[]’ to an 
agency the authority to give meaning to a particrdar statutory term.” Under 
those circumstances, “the statute’s meaning may well be that the agency is 
authorized to exercise a degree of discretion.” Among the statutes cited by the 
Court to support this proposition was 29 U.S.C. § 213(a)(15), which exempts 
from provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act “any employee employed on a 
casual basis in domestic service employment to provide companionship 
services for individuals who (because of age or infirmity) are unable to care for 
themselves (as such terms are defined and delimited by regulations of the 
Secretary).” (Emphasis added by Loper Bright}
Imagine that, instead of an ambiguous statute, the Court confronts a 
regulation with ambiguous terms, along with a regulatory instruction that 
those terms should be construed “as defined and delimited by further 
interpretive rules issued by the Secretary.” Would such a regulation “expressly 
delegate” intei?pretive authority to a future Secretary “to give meaning to a 
particular [regulatory] term”? If so, agencies could expressly adopt the 
approach of Auer deference by using such language, irrespective of whether the 
Court decides in the future that Auer deference generally con flirts with Section 
706 of the APA. But a regulation that adopted such language might, perhaps, 
prompt another constitutional challenge akin to the one rejected in Kisor or 
the one left unadressed in Loper Bright.
